item.title: @SemiconductorsX：NAND现货价格因需求放缓下滑，市场对DRAM合约价走势存在分歧
item.description:
DRAM prices are still expected to rise next year. A data-center slowdown could reverse that quickly.
$DRAM
NAND spot prices already dropped. The TLC 512Gb wafer averaged $14.267 on November 9, down 11.67% from $16.152 on November 2. Chinese CSP cuts to enterprise SSD orders drove the move.

TrendForce sees NAND bit supply up 25-30% next year. Contract prices are projected to fall 0-5% quarter-on-quarter in both the first and second quarters. Weaker smartphone and PC demand plus lower storage per device add pressure.

Samsung and SK Hynix sell most volume to North American big tech on contract prices. Spot drops do not hit their results the same way.
$SKHY
TrendForce still sees general DRAM contract prices rising 5-10% in the first quarter, 3-8% in the second, and 0-5% in the third and fourth. The turning point sits around mid-2028.

Counterpoint sees growth lasting into the first half of 2027. Supply growth and slower demand later could still force a sharp adjustment if the balance shifts earlier. BNK’s Lee Min-hee estimates 2026 DRAM bit demand up 24% while supplier shipments rise 38%.

That gap could build inventory and trigger a steep price drop from the second or third quarter of next year if end demand weakens. No official cut in server DRAM content has appeared yet.

New cleanrooms and lines from SK Hynix and Samsung open between 2027 and 2029. Actual output lags. Third-quarter global DRAM revenue rose 369% year-on-year while bit shipments rose only about 4%. Earnings lean heavily on price.

SK Hynix has LTAs with 14 customers covering more than 50% of 2027-2028 production. Samsung said its 2027 HBM volume is fully sold at agreed prices.

SoftBank booked a 597.2 billion yen loss after canceling a US data-center power contract. Full memory cancellations still look unlikely while AI competition and tight supply continue.

How much of the 2027 DRAM contract rise survives if Chinese CSP order cuts spread from NAND into server DRAM?

item.title: @SemiconductorsX：韩国KDI上调明后两年经济增长预测，半导体占今年增长贡献近一半
item.description:
Korea’s growth is running in the high 3% range. Semiconductors are carrying most of it.

KDI now sees 2026 GDP growth at 3.8% and 2027 at 3.9%. Those are up 0.6 and 1.7 percentage points from the August forecast.

The IMF raised its figures to 3.9% this year and 3.3% next year. Two straight years above 3% would be the first since 2013–2014.

Semiconductors accounted for about half of this year’s growth contribution. Next year they are expected to make up two-thirds of the 3.9% pace. The concentration leaves the economy exposed if global AI spending cools or the memory cycle turns.

Job gains stay weak. KDI expects only 120,000 more employed this year, the smallest rise since 2018 outside the COVID drop.

January–October employment rose by a monthly average of 119,000, but health and social welfare added 227,000 while other sectors lost 108,000.

Manufacturing output rose 7.0% in the third quarter. Manufacturing employment fell by a monthly average of 31,000.

In October, total employment rose 139,000, yet the under-60 group fell 57,000. Youth employment (15–29) dropped 196,000 for the 48th straight month. The youth employment rate stands at 42.9%.

How much of the 2027 growth holds if semiconductor contribution stays near two-thirds and manufacturing jobs keep shrinking?

item.title: @charles_irl：行业观点称GTA 6采用GPU驱动软件渲染与网格及计算着色器实现极致图形规模与复杂度
item.description:
GTA VI is a megakernel

@timsoret：In fact, I do understand, it's just that I'm astounded by the sheer scope & quality that has been achieved.

GTA VI is the ultimate victoy of GPU-driven software rendering, relying on tons of mesh shaders & compute shaders.

At the cost of higher complexity, these pipelines make the GPU manage its own workload. It's the only way to cull millions of instances per frame & to stream virtualized geometry.

Otherwise, it's the CPU slowly dispatching draw calls, figuring out what to draw with bounding box culling. It's crude, slow, imprecise and doesn't scale.

We already saw the birth of GPU software rendering in the past thanks to compute shaders:
- Assassin's Creed Unity had GPU culling
- Demon's Souls remake showcased impressive software tesselation
- UE5's brought virtualized geometry with Nanite & Lumen
- Alan Wake 2 & Assassin's Creed Shadows went full GPU-driven rendering

1. Progress on verifiable tasks continues. In particular, improving the cost efficiency of existing capabilities is a highly verifiable task. For the past few years, cost per equivalent capability has dropped by at least 10x per year. I think this progress will be sustained for a few more years, and even accelerate as labs use AI more and more heavily for AI research in the pursuit of RSI. There is of course a ceiling to efficiency improvements, but I don’t think we’re close to that ceiling.

item.description:
I've had tons of discussions around LLM judges since working on a benchmark myself.

Turns out, a lot of people overcomplicate LLM judges before they even have a solid prompt.

A collaborator and I were planning our workshop session on ToneBench, and we made a deliberate choice: keep it skills-focused rather than deep AI engineering.

When people build automated evaluation systems, the temptation is to jump straight into complex multi-agent architectures and scoring math.

In reality, getting reliable evaluations comes down to a tight prompt iteration loop.

You write clear evaluation criteria, run the judge against real drafts, find where it misinterprets tone or nuance, and refine the instructions.

Each iteration teaches you more about your edge cases than an elaborate pipeline ever could.

If your LLM judge is giving erratic scores, do not add more infrastructure.

Fix the criteria and tighten the feedback loop first.

The most important part that needs your time is the human calibration. Build this set as soon as you can and use it to iterate with your LLM judges.

But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal.

@ObhishekSaha：Like most mathematicians, I believed the Riemann Hypothesis to be completely out of reach at present (even with the best AI tools), because I expected it to require substantial theory-building, probably in arithmetic geometry. The kind of new theory-building that fills entire books, and that AI isn't so good at yet.

Mathematicians have a notion of how deep a problem is. A sufficiently deep problem is generally intractable until enough of the theory is in place. If difficult problems are like valuable mineral reserves buried miles underground, you first need to build the infrastructure to reach them.

What Levent's proof seems to have done instead is something completely different. It takes an incredibly complicated tour through the infrastructure built for a hundred other mineral reserves, situated far from the destination, and somehow create a wormhole to the original destination.

This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.

I think trying to track how much work AI can do autonomously is critical, and this is a useful counter to some of the most audacious claims about the state of autonomous AI research. But I do want to note that the focus on research tasks at the most advanced AI research organizations on the planet also runs the risk of substantially underestimating what AI can already do in terms of economically valuable tasks. Its worth separating the two (and I don't think Ramez is claiming they are not seperated).

Most work is not frontier AI research, and there AI can be tremendously successful. Epoch's MirrorCode results, for example, show AI autonomously reimplementing software that the researchers estimate would take a humans 2-17 weeks. This is well-specified work, so it has very different boundary conditions.

Plus, in the real world, some human intervention is fine (in my mind, vastly preferrable to no human role for a variety of reasons). Occasional guidance can still leave you with enormous productivity gains, even if that doesn’t satisfy the requirements for fully autonomous AI research. And even in the case of AI research, the same OpenAI report includes researchers estimating that a month of their team’s work would have taken three months without coding agents, on average.

In short, RSI/AI-driven research progress may not tightly couple with progress on economically valuable tasks, and the variance and range on those tasks are less well understood.

item.title: @testingcatalog：谷歌推出名为Loop的新型自适应人工智能代理，旨在实现自主协同工作与任务管理
item.description:
Google recently announced Loop, its new self-improving AI agent that can autonomously work toward a given goal.

Loop is internally called Jitro; interestingly, that was the exact name for Jules v2.

Here is how it works 👀

1. Users start creating a Workspace by connecting it to a selected Github project and adding basic information.

2. Users can create loops manually or select ones that are already predefined (ex., Harden Application Security)

"Custom Loops" can be created via a prompt or by manually filling in the Loop title, icon, and objective.

> "Loops are mid- to long-term objectives for Stitch Loop to continuously work toward. They can range from highly specific to broad, but should always be something code can achieve," says the description.

3. Users can connect additional context in the form of Integrations, Files, Links, or additional repositories.

More than 100 integrations are available there, including services like Jira, Linear, Datadog, Sentry, Notion, Snowflake, Salesforce, Intercom, Discord, Slack, Figma, and many others.

Custom MCPs are supported as well.

4. After creating a workspace, Loop will start digging into your project details and generate its own Skills about the product and product metrics.

These Skills will live in a separate tab and can be edited in the UI in Markdown.

5. When the Workspace is ready, Loop will suggest metrics and goals based on its own research. Users can convert these suggestions into loops right away.

When a Loop is created, it appears as a running process in the main UI.

6. When a Loop is finished, users will see a list of suggestions for every loop, along with a number associated with a target metric and progress status.

Example Loop:
- Goal - Scale Telegram community contributions.
- KPIs - community members, registered contributors, active members.

A high-level goal would be broken down into sub-KPIs. When users open a dedicated Loop page, all these KPIs will be visible on the dashboard.

Below, Users will see a list of Tasks, Skills, and Activity tabs.

Example Task:
- Telegram channel lacks discussion threads and a dedicated bot.

Each task has a detailed description, labels, and the date when it was updated. Below, users will see tabs for Solutions, Activity, and Evidence.

Activity appears as a summary describing what happened, what was done, and the general Timeline.

Evidence contains links to where Loop pulled the context behind this Task. In my example case, it refers to the TestingCatalog website and the Telegram channel from which it pulled all the numbers.

Example Solution:
- Dedicated Telegram Bot API intake bot with editorial triage webhook (implementation task).

This task is an implementation task that has a clear description, Impact, scope, and Risk labeled.

Users can start the task right from this page to begin solution development via Gemini.

When the task is done, users can review its progress and status and monitor its impact on production by pulling updated metrics and KPIs after the release.

What does all this mean? 🤯

Loop follows how "Product work" is done at Google, a model many other companies also use.

Every Workspace in Loop is equivalent to a scope that is normally handled by a complete product engineering team.

It is no longer a place where users play the role of engineering lead and product lead, orchestrating AI agents.

It is a place where the user plays the role of a senior manager managing several engineering teams, which is a big shift on its own.

We are slowly moving towards autonomous AI organizations. One management layer at a time.

I expect it will still take until 2027 for labs to develop the products and models needed to make substantial progress in this area (assuming AI continues to advance in a semi-regulated format as it is now).
